newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lagerfeld, slammed over fur, shows his last Chloe.
newsitem.headline: Lagerfeld, slammed over fur, shows his last Chloe.

text.p: German designer Karl Lagerfeld presented his final collection for the house of Chloe on Friday as animal rights activists in the nude lambasted him for using fur in his fashion designs.

Although fox, mink and rabbit were back in full force at Christian Dior, John Galliano, Givenchy and many other houses this week, Lagerfeld was the target of a protest outside his offices by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) because of his work for Fendi, Italy's largest fur purveyor.
His shows for Chanel and Chloe this week were animal-friendly.

"While famous designers like Giorgio Armani, Oleg Cassini, Calvin Klein and Donna Karan never work with fur, Karl Lagerfeld remains a fashion dinosaur," said Violet Kelly, one of three women who stood stark naked on a major Paris thoroughfare, made up as leopards and shielded solely by a banner reading "Fur is only for Animals".
Kelly also criticised supermodel Naomi Campbell, who posed nude in a PETA ad campaign in 1993, for modeling one of Lagerfeld's fur coats at the last week's Fendi show in Milan.

Meanwhile Lagerfeld's Chloe farewell on an intergalactic stage set was a soft 1970s look in skirty velvet coats with puffy sleeves, fluid bellbottoms in a palette of mauve, plum, tangerine and jellybean pink.

He crafted pastel plaid blankets for wraparound skirts, domino-print chiffons into empoire dresses and cubist mohair for dustcoats. Solar system stars twinkled against flowing midnight blue evening wear and fur was all fake on candy-striped jackets.

"I thought it was very Karl, with a million ideas. Good," said Joan Kaner of U.S. department stores Neiman Marcus. "It had his essence and yet the message of the season which was really, anything goes."

The house of Chloe said in a statement that Lagerfeld's departure was a "mutual decision dictated by time constraints" and to devote more time to his signature line, his work at Chanel and his photography.
On Thursday night, British designer John Galliano's fashion vision for next winter was all Egyptian empresses in safety pins and pubescent school girls with hormones kicking in.
A flurry of prep school uniforms turned racy, their grey flannel jackets squeezing nubile curves and pleated skirts clipped as high as the supermodel's underthings.
Then the pleated skirts became Egyptian loincloths and the models coiffed and made-up as Cleopatra, with snakeskin sandals that wound up the leg, and cobras staring from scaly golden head-dresses.
It was pure, pulsing theatre, from a tartan coat and bellbottoms swimming under a sea of brass buttons, to a heart- stopping liquid gold gown with gilt hands clasping the breasts.

There was Galliano's vintage romanticism in sumptuous bias- cut chiffon with ruffles dribbling in spirals around the body, and irreverent humour in a Union Jack toga or transparent body stockings with a portrait of Jesus down the back.
But oversexed Egyptian queens are no longer of this age and few are the women who can find an occasion, let alone the cash, to wear his otherworldly catwalk creations.
Joseph Boitano of exclusive department store Bergdorf Goodman said that under all of the theatrical paraphernalia, there were also down to earth clothes for today's woman.
"It's an amazing spectacle, very exciting and so much creativity. I'm certain that in the showroom , it will be put together in way that's wearable," he told Reuters.
"But the spirit is what's really important. John can come up with so many ideas, and it's amazingly executed," Boitano added.
